He explains how the court assessed evidence of genocidal intent, rejecting Myanmar's justification of its military operations as counterterrorism. He argues that "the existence of an armed conflict or a security objective doesn't exclude genocidal intent," a finding he believes will have "far-reaching implications in future genocide cases," including South Africa's case against Israel over Gaza. Brody also discusses the Gambia's role in bringing the case and growing challenges to international accountability, warning that "we're in a very dangerous moment."

events.title: UNICEF Somalia Humanitarian Situation Report No.3, 1 July - 30 September 2026
events.summary: Country: Somalia Source: UN Children's Fund Please refer to the attached file. Highlights Somalia's humanitarian needs remained high during the quarter, driven by drought, conflict, displacement, disease outbreaks and declining humanitarian assistance. An estimated 5.1 million people faced acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3+), while 1.92 million children were projected to suffer acute malnutrition between July 2026 and June 2027. About 75,000 displacement movements and over 1,400 conflict events were recorded. UNICEF sustained lifesaving assistance across priority sectors, reaching 98,241 children with SAM treatment, 244,022 caregivers with IYCF counselling, 145,671 people with primary health care, and 286,006 people with safe water. Education support benefited 71,644 children, while 48,991 people accessed child protection services. Monthly cash transfers supported 13,493 vulnerable women, strengthening household resilience. The 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal was 27 per cent funded (US$32 million) against US$121 million required, leaving a US$89 million gap. Underfunding continued to constrain service coverage, operational capacity and emergency preparedness for anticipated El Nino impacts.

More children than ever live in conflict zones Posted Thursday, 19 Nov 2026 by Gudrun Østby & Siri Aas Rustad More children now live near armed conflict than the combined populations of the United States, Canada and Mexico. Armed violence escalated sharply across the globe in 2025. Data from the Uppsala Conflict Data Program (UCDP) shows that conflict-related fatalities rose to 244,600, up from approximately 187,000 in 2024. This made 2025 one of the deadliest years since the end of the Cold War. Much of the increase was driven by a dramatic rise in violence targeting civilians, particularly in Sudan. While armed conflict affects entire populations, children are among those who suffer the most severe and lasting consequences. Children face grave violations , including killing and maiming, recruitment by armed groups, sexual violence, abduction, attacks on schools and hospitals, and denial of humanitarian access. But the consequences of war extend far beyond direct violence. Children living in conflict-affected areas are more likely to drop out of school, lack access to clean water, and face heightened risks of death from illness, malnutrition, or lack of vaccines and medical care. Today, Save the Children launches its new report, Stop the War on Children 2026 . The report is based on PRIO’s tenth annual mapping of children in armed conflict covering the period 1990–2025. Our latest estimates show that 589 million children, more than one in five of the world's children, were living in conflict zones in 2025 . UNFPA warns: the world risks letting the next generation down A mix of economic instability, inequality, exclusion and other destabilizing factors are holding young people back from fulfilling their ambitions. The figure represents an increase of more than 50% in a decade, jumping from 378 million in 2015 to 589 million in 2025, according to the report Stop the War on Children: Changing the Odds , which draws on data from the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO). The report found that the share of the world’s children living in conflict zones more than doubled from about 10% in the mid-1990s to 23.4% in 2025. Africa is home to the highest number of children living in conflict zones, accounting for about 260 million, or 44% of the global total. This is nearly a 20% increase from the 218 million children in Africa who lived in conflict zones in 2024. Across Africa, the proportion of children living in conflict zones more than tripled from about one in eight children in 2010 to about two in five in 2025, the highest level ever recorded for the continent. This puts Africa on par with the Middle East, where both regions now have two in five children living in conflict zones. Los informes se centran en dos importantes países que acogen refugiados, Bangladés y Etiopía , cada uno de los cuales acoge a más de un millón de personas refugiadas y solicitantes de asilo.
